metadata.title: Mixture of Experts.
metadata.note: Standalone teaching explainer (~2.5min) on Mixture of Experts (MoE). FRAMEWORK-FIRST (built to pass PROOF): the definition (B01: many experts + a router, only a few run) and the reframe (B02: total vs active params) are shown before the worked example (B03: one token routed to top-2 experts); then the trade/falsifiability (B04: all experts in memory, routing imbalance, not 'smarter'); scaffolded task (B06). ONE insight: MoE pulls CAPACITY apart from COST — total params (all experts, in memory) vs active params (the few that run per token). DOUBLE-CHECK LAW: no parameter counts, benchmarks, or model names; top-2 routing used as an illustrative typical. Bookends render (composer/verdict/handoff/outro via Claude Remotion comps); body B01-B04 are house-style 4K PIL cards generated by make_cards.py.

beats.narration_text: Hey, I'm Muskan. Some AI models are enormous, hundreds of billions of parameters, yet they run about as cheaply as a much smaller one. How? They don't use all of themselves at once. That trick has a name: Mixture of Experts. Let's see how it splits a giant model into parts that take turns.

props.command: How can a model have hundreds of billions of parameters but run as cheap as a small one?
output: only a few run per token

beats.narration_text: Here's the idea. A normal, dense model runs every one of its parameters for every token. A Mixture of Experts model instead has many smaller expert networks, plus a little router. For each token, the router picks just a few experts to run, and the rest sit idle. Same token, but only a slice of the model actually does the work.

show.event: the four definition cards snap in

card.title: Many Experts, One Router.
card.subtitle: the model takes turns with itself
card.caption: a dense model runs every parameter every token — an MoE runs only a slice
card.footer: EXPERTS + A ROUTER · A SLICE RUNS, NOT THE WHOLE

beats.narration_text: This splits one number we usually treat as one. Total parameters: every expert added up, that's the model's capacity, and it all has to live in memory. Active parameters: just the few experts that run for a given token, that's the compute, and the speed. An MoE model can be huge in total, while staying small in active. Capacity and cost, pulled apart.

card.title: Total vs Active.
card.subtitle: one number, pulled apart
card.caption: an MoE can be enormous in total while staying small in active

beats.narration_text: Watch one token go through. The router scores the experts and sends the token to the top two, say, out of dozens. Only those two compute; their outputs are combined into the result. The next token might go to two completely different experts. So the model keeps all its knowledge available, but pays for only a sliver of it each step.

show.event: the answer resolves: top-2 run, combined (accent)

card.title: One Token, Two Experts.
card.subtitle: how routing works
card.answer: scores the experts → sends it to the top 2 → only those compute, outputs combined
card.caption: the next token might pick two completely different experts
card.footer: TOP-k OF MANY · ONLY THE CHOSEN RUN

beats.narration_text: But it's not a free lunch. Every expert still has to sit in memory, even the ones not running, so an MoE model is memory-hungry and hard to serve. The router can get lopsided, overusing a few experts and wasting the rest, which needs extra training tricks to balance. And it's not smarter, it's cheaper per token for the capacity. You're trading memory and complexity for compute.

show.event: the four trade cards snap in

card.title: Not a Free Lunch.
card.subtitle: what MoE costs

items.quote: every expert in memory — even idle ones
cheaper per token, for the capacity

card.caption: all experts must be held even though only a few run — MoE is memory-hungry to serve
card.footer: SMALL ACTIVE COMPUTE · LARGE TOTAL MEMORY

beats.narration_text: So, Mixture of Experts: many experts, a router that picks a few per token, and only those run. It pulls capacity apart from cost, a huge model you pay for a slice at a time. The catch is memory, you still have to hold all the experts.

artifactLines: A dense model runs every parameter per token; an MoE has many experts + a router that picks a few.
Only the chosen experts run, so compute per token stays small even as total capacity grows huge.
Read two numbers: total params (capacity, all in memory) vs active params (compute + speed).
The catch: every expert must live in memory, and routing can imbalance — you trade memory for compute.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Next time you read that a model has some gigantic parameter count, ask the second question: how many of those are active per token? If it's an MoE, the active number, the one that sets speed and cost, is far smaller. Learning to read total versus active tells you what a model will actually cost to run.

props.command: Next time a model boasts a giant parameter count, ask: how many params are ACTIVE per token? If it's an MoE, which number sets its real speed and cost — total, or active?

beats.narration_text: Mixture of Experts. Capacity, apart from cost. Humanitarians AI.
